lesson.title: __init__: The Setup Call Every New Object Gets
lesson.summary: __init__ is a special method that Python calls automatically the moment a new object is created, giving you one guaranteed place to set up its starting attributes.
lesson.body:
When you write fido.name = "Fido" as a separate line right after creating a Dog, you're relying on remembering to do that setup every single time, for every single object, and for every attribute the object needs. Forget one line, or create the object in a different order, and you end up with objects that are missing data they should always have. Python solves this with a special method: __init__. If a class defines a method named __init__, Python calls it automatically, immediately, every time a new object of that class is created, and it's the natural home for setup code.

__init__ works like any other method: its first parameter is self, referring to the brand new object being built, and after that you can list whatever parameters you want, using everything you already know about writing parameters for ordinary functions. Whatever values get passed in when the object is created flow straight into __init__, and from there you attach them to self so they stick around as attributes of that object.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

fido = Dog("Fido", 3)
print(fido.name)
# Output: Fido
print(fido.age)
# Output: 3
```

Trace it step by step. The line Dog("Fido", 3) tells Python to build a new Dog and immediately call __init__ on it, with self bound to that new object, name bound to "Fido", and age bound to 3. Inside the method, self.name = name creates an attribute called name on the new object and stores "Fido" in it; self.age = age does the same for age with the value 3. By the time that line finishes, fido already has both attributes fully set, with no extra setup lines required anywhere else in your program. print(fido.name) then simply reads that stored value back out and prints Fido, and print(fido.age) prints 3.

Two details are worth locking in now, because students trip on them constantly. First, __init__ never has a return statement that hands back a value; its whole job is to configure the object that already exists, not to produce a result, and Python will actually raise a TypeError if you try to make it return anything other than None. Second, the double underscores on either side of init are not decoration, they mark this as one of Python's "dunder" (double underscore) methods, a category of special methods that Python itself calls automatically under specific circumstances rather than methods you call by hand. You will never write fido.__init__("Rex", 5) yourself in ordinary code; Python invokes it for you the moment you write Dog("Fido", 3).
